---
title: "Readings — Targeted sequencing"
---

Reading is optional but each item is here for a reason. Start with the two marked **start here**.

## Papers

**Mamanova L, et al. (2010).** *Target-enrichment strategies for next-generation sequencing.*
Nature Methods 7:111–118.
[doi:10.1038/nmeth.1419](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmeth.1419) — **start here**

> A map of the whole field: PCR, capture, circularising probes. Use it to place each method in the three-way split from the lecture.

**Gnirke A, et al. (2009).** *Solution hybrid selection with ultra-long oligonucleotides for massively
parallel targeted sequencing.* Nature Biotechnology 27:182–189.
[doi:10.1038/nbt.1523](https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.1523)

> The solution-phase capture that SureSelect-type kits descend from. Note the role of blockers and of the hybridisation conditions.

**Hiatt JB, et al. (2013).** *Single molecule molecular inversion probes for targeted, high-accuracy
detection of low-frequency variation.* Genome Research 23:843–854.
[doi:10.1101/gr.147686.112](https://doi.org/10.1101/gr.147686.112)

> How a random tag in a circularising probe gives molecule-level consensus. Compare the error suppression with the untagged case.

**Kinde I, et al. (2011).** *Detection and quantification of rare mutations with massively parallel
sequencing.* PNAS 108:9530–9535.
[doi:10.1073/pnas.1105422108](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1105422108) — **start here**

> Safe-SeqS: the clearest statement of why unique identifiers beat depth. Look at what the error rate was before and after.

**Schmitt MW, et al. (2012).** *Detection of ultra-rare mutations by next-generation sequencing.*
PNAS 109:14508–14513.
[doi:10.1073/pnas.1208715109](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1208715109)

> Duplex sequencing. Follow how the two strands are linked and what is rejected.

**Newman AM, et al. (2014).** *An ultrasensitive method for quantitating circulating tumor DNA with
broad patient coverage.* Nature Medicine 20:548–554.
[doi:10.1038/nm.3519](https://doi.org/10.1038/nm.3519)

> CAPP-Seq: a population-informed selector. The question to ask is how a design for the cancer type, not the patient, still works for most patients.

**Meissner A, et al. (2008).** *Genome-scale DNA methylation maps of pluripotent and differentiated cells.*
Nature 454:766–770.
[doi:10.1038/nature07107](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature07107)

> RRBS as it was introduced. Read the methods for the order of digest, adapter ligation and bisulfite.

**Gilpatrick T, et al. (2020).** *Targeted nanopore sequencing with Cas9-guided adapter ligation.*
Nature Biotechnology 38:433–438.
[doi:10.1038/s41587-020-0407-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-020-0407-5)

> Cas9 as a selection step with no amplification.

## Reference material to keep open

- [NGS_101 collection](https://henriksson-lab.github.io/NGS_101/): CAPP-Seq, SureSelect XT HS2, smMIP, Safe-SeqS, Duplex Sequencing, RRBS, ARTIC tiled amplicons
- [NEB selection charts](https://www.neb.com/en/tools-and-resources/selection-charts)
